subtitle: The wires and waves that carry bits, and the arithmetic that notices, fixes and shrinks them.

guided.body:
Pick up the network cable behind your computer. What is inside it, and why? There are three main kinds of wire, and each is a trade of cost for capability.

Twisted pair (UTP/STP): two insulated wires twisted to cancel interference. It is cheap and the LAN workhorse (Cat 5e/6, up to 100 m). Coaxial: a centre conductor inside a shield, with higher bandwidth, as in cable TV. Optical fibre: light in a glass core by total internal reflection, with enormous bandwidth and low loss, and it is immune to electrical noise; single-mode for long haul, multimode for short runs. As the figure shows, bandwidth and distance rise left to right, and so does the cost. Why is fibre immune to electromagnetic interference? Because it carries light, not electricity.
keynotes: Twisted pair is two insulated wires twisted to cancel interference: cheap, the LAN workhorse (Cat 5e/6, up to 100 m).
Coaxial has a centre conductor inside a shield, with higher bandwidth, as in cable TV.
Optical fibre carries light by total internal reflection with enormous bandwidth and low loss, immune to electrical noise; single-mode for long haul, multimode for short runs.

unguided.body:
No wire at all? You may be surprised that the air can carry signals too. Radio waves are omnidirectional and pass through walls. Microwaves are line-of-sight, dish to dish, and also used by satellites. Infrared is short range and blocked by walls.

Waves travel in three ways. Ground wave: low frequencies follow the earth. Sky wave: HF reflects off the ionosphere for long distance. Line of sight: VHF and above, limited by the horizon. A rule to remember: higher frequencies carry more data but travel less far. So microwaves and satellite links use line of sight.
keynotes: Radio waves are omnidirectional and pass walls; microwaves are line-of-sight; infrared is short range and blocked by walls.
Propagation modes: ground wave (low frequencies), sky wave (HF reflects off the ionosphere) and line of sight (VHF and above).
Higher frequencies carry more data but travel less far.

errors.body:
Noise flips bits, and a flipped bit can turn “pay Rs 100” into “pay Rs 900”. How do you notice? With three increasingly clever tricks. A single parity bit detects any odd number of errors, but misses an even number. A checksum sums the data words and sends the complement. The CRC divides by a generator polynomial with XOR and sends the remainder: for data 1101011011 and generator 10011 the CRC is 1110.

Watch the long division with XOR in the figure. A single even-parity bit cannot detect an even number of bit errors, because two flips cancel out.
keynotes: A single parity bit detects any odd number of errors.
A checksum sums the data words and sends the complement.
The CRC divides by a generator polynomial with XOR and sends the remainder: data 1101011011 with generator 10011 gives 1110.

ham.body:
Detecting an error is good; fixing it without asking for a resend is magic, and Hamming found a way. Put extra parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4, 8…, and let the receiver locate a single error: the failed checks, read as binary, name the position. Encode 1011 and you get 0110011; flip bit 5 and the syndrome is 5, pointing straight at the culprit.

How powerful is a code? Its minimum Hamming distance d decides: it detects d−1 errors and corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋. A code with minimum distance 5 detects d − 1 = 4 errors and corrects ⌊4/2⌋ = 2. With distance 3, you can correct one error.
keynotes: Extra parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4, 8… let the receiver locate a single error: the failed checks, read as binary, name the position.
1011 encodes as 0110011, and flipping bit 5 gives syndrome 5.
A minimum Hamming distance d detects d−1 errors and corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋; d = 5 detects 4 and corrects 2.

comp.body:
Can we send fewer bits for the same message? Yes, and there are two philosophies. Lossless compression removes redundancy and reproduces the data exactly (ZIP, PNG) using run-length coding, Huffman and Lempel–Ziv. Lossy compression discards what perception will not miss (JPEG, MP3), for much higher ratios.

Huffman is delightful: frequent symbols get short codes, like abbreviating the words you use most. The message aaaabbc needs 10 bits instead of 56. The merge order builds the tree in the figure. Which format is lossy? JPEG, since it throws details away.
keynotes: Lossless compression removes redundancy and reproduces the data exactly (ZIP, PNG): run-length coding, Huffman and Lempel–Ziv.
Lossy compression discards what perception will not miss (JPEG, MP3) for much higher ratios.
Huffman gives frequent symbols short codes: aaaabbc needs 10 bits instead of 56.

summary.body:
Three lines before you move on.

  • Twisted pair → coax → fibre: more bandwidth, more cost.
  • CRC detects; Hamming corrects one error; distance d detects d−1, corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋.
  • Lossless keeps every bit; lossy trades fidelity for size.
keynotes: Twisted pair, coax and fibre give more bandwidth at more cost.
CRC detects, Hamming corrects one error, and distance d detects d−1 and corrects ⌊(d−1)/2⌋.
Lossless keeps every bit; lossy trades fidelity for size.
